entities.summary: Francis La Flesche was the first professional Native American ethnologist; he worked with the Smithsonian Institution. He specialized in Omaha and Osage cultures. Working closely as a translator and researcher with the anthropologist Alice C. Fletcher, La Flesche wrote several articles and a book on the Omaha, plus more numerous works on the Osage. He made valuable original recordings of their traditional songs and chants. Beginning in 1908, he collaborated with American composer Charles Wakefield Cadman to develop an opera, Da O Ma (1912), based on his stories of Omaha life, but it was never produced.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: As the first professional Native American ethnologist, Francis La Flesche's work with Alice C. Fletcher and Charles Wakefield Cadman helped document and preserve Omaha and Osage cultures through his writings and recordings. His contributions to the field of anthropology paved the way for future generations of researchers.
